title: Human Enhancement Technologies: Ethics, Liberty, Coercion, and Governance
content: Human enhancement technologies seek to improve capacities such as memory, mood, strength, endurance, sensory function, longevity, and resistance to disease. Their ethical evaluation is often framed as a dispute between transhumanist enthusiasm and bioconservative caution, but that binary can obscure the practical questions that should govern policy. This essay argues that enhancement should not be judged primarily by whether it is natural or whether it falls on the therapeutic side of a therapy–enhancement boundary. More useful criteria are safety, proportionality, voluntariness, reversibility, effects on identity and agency, distributive fairness, risks of coercion, commercial dependence, dual-use potential, and the quality of public oversight. These criteria are applied to pharmacologic and electrical neuroenhancement, brain–computer interfaces, human genome editing, military enhancement, and life extension. Some enhancements may represent legitimate extensions of medicine and human freedom; others may create new forms of inequality, manipulation, and domination. A defensible response is therefore neither categorical prohibition nor technological enthusiasm, but accountable, evidence-based governance that protects both individual liberty and the conditions of a just society.
